title: Reflection symmetry organizes zeros without forcing the critical line
claim: Completion makes the reflection s↔1-s comparable across L-functions, while the Eisenstein setting further separates spectral reflection from modular symmetry; the Davenport-Heilbronn calibration shows that a Riemann-type functional equation can coexist with off-line zeros. The shared mechanism therefore organizes zero pairing and proof interfaces but is not itself a line-zero criterion.
historical_or_program_relation: This connects the family-level completion viewpoint to later function-specific zero theorems and Speiser diagnostics by treating symmetry as infrastructure whose sufficiency must be tested, not as a surrogate for RH.
limits: The sources do not identify the completed functions, make modular and spectral symmetry interchangeable, or show that every function with reflection symmetry satisfies the same Speiser theorem; the Davenport-Heilbronn comparison is a class-specific calibration.

title: Equivalent criteria preserve truth while relocating the infinite burden
claim: The all-degree Jensen hierarchy, the universally quantified Nicolas inequalities, and one-target membership in a closed natural-dilation span replace the same zero-location question by different infinite obligations: simultaneous hyperbolicity, every-cutoff order, and Hilbert-space closure. Logical equivalence does not select which representation exposes a tractable obstruction.
historical_or_program_relation: The concrete criteria instantiate the historical warning that equivalent formulations can become a strategic black hole: the decisive research choice is the proof burden made visible by the representation, not equivalence alone.
limits: This relation neither ranks the criteria nor supplies direct implications among them except through their reported RH equivalences; finite degree checks, sampled cutoffs, and finite approximants do not discharge their respective global quantifiers.

title: Mellin evaluation turns closure into a zero-exclusion witness
claim: Across deterministic, kernel-generalized, and probabilistic Nyman-Beurling routes, Mellin coordinates expose zeta-weighted dilation structure and convert approximation into zero exclusion: at a putative off-critical zero the approximants retain a fixed transform constraint, while norm convergence and a continuity mechanism force passage to the target. Compact-support mean cancellation and a physical-scale tail split are two different ways of making that evaluation continuous.
historical_or_program_relation: The later variants preserve the original closure-to-zero contradiction while changing how the analytic continuity obligation is certified, revealing an invariant proof skeleton beneath different approximation models.
limits: The compactification and tail-splitting arguments have different hypotheses and are not interchangeable; the generalized-kernel result yields zero-set inclusion and still needs kernel-transform nonvanishing, while probabilistic exclusion depends on its stated approximation and tail controls.

title: Changing the dilation dictionary moves the obstruction rather than removing it
claim: Restricting continuous dilations to natural indices, varying the underlying strong kernel, or randomizing dilation parameters all redesign the approximation dictionary. The cross-source constraint is that expressivity must still reach the distinguished target: discrete sufficiency is a theorem to prove, kernel synthesis is limited by unknown additive closure, and probabilistic families face a geometric obstruction when fine scales are inaccessible.
historical_or_program_relation: These extensions turn Nyman-Beurling from one fixed family into a controlled study of which scale dictionaries retain the closure mechanism, with exponential and concentrating Gamma laws probing analytically distinct routes.
limits: Random, deterministic, and kernel-generated spans are not asserted equal; the smallest-scale lower bound does not characterize total approximation error, and dilation stability of strong kernels does not make them a linear design space.

title: An exponential transform transfers the Riesz growth threshold to finite-difference decay
claim: The Riesz criterion compresses reciprocal zeta samples into an entire-series growth observable, while the exponential generating relation transfers its RH-scale exponent to decay of the Baez-Duarte finite-difference sequence. The later trend-plus-zero decomposition explains how global coefficient cancellation can appear as spectral oscillation, and direct high-precision evaluation supplies an independent numerical check on that faster representation.
historical_or_program_relation: This is a refinement from a continuous entire-function criterion to a discrete sequence with an explicit transform and then to a spectral decomposition, making both the asymptotic signal and its computational conditioning visible.
limits: The zero-based decomposition is an analysis or computation channel under its stated assumptions, not an independent proof of RH; catastrophic cancellation means naive finite-difference numerics cannot certify the required asymptotic bound, and no finite computation settles it.

title: Elementary criteria concentrate RH in signed secondary errors
claim: Divisor-sum, prime-cutoff, and Farey formulations first remove or align dominant growth and then ask a signed secondary term to stay within a universal square-root- or lower-order envelope. Exact positive remainders, bounded coordinate changes, and finite-plus-tail partitions can preserve the needed inequality, whereas matching limiting constants without a one-sided rate cannot.
historical_or_program_relation: The programs progressively translate analytic zero location into elementary arithmetic observables, but their common proof architecture is threshold calibration: the main term is not the battleground once the criterion has been normalized.
limits: The observables and normalizations are not interchangeable, bounded Farey error transfers only the stated asymptotic scale, and the Nicolas/Dedekind factor synthesis explicitly retains a proof gap because complementary limits do not imply the required eventual inequality.

title: Finite agreement becomes relevant only through a stability theorem
claim: Line-supported zeros of finite-prime minimizers and eventual hyperbolicity of every fixed Jensen degree are strong local or finite-regime facts, but each leaves a distinct global passage open. The former needs compact-uniform convergence so Hurwitz can transport zero geometry; the latter does not replace the simultaneous all-degree hyperbolicity required by the RH equivalence.
historical_or_program_relation: The two programs expose the same methodological boundary in different representations: finite objects can suggest the correct geometry, but a named topology or uniformity principle must carry that geometry to the infinite target.
limits: The sources do not identify the minimizers with Jensen polynomials or reduce one convergence problem to the other; eventual fixed-degree results and decimal finite-prime agreement remain evidence for their own programs, not proofs of RH.

title: Random-matrix agreement is obtained only after a controlled loss of global information
claim: Random-matrix behavior enters through representations designed for distributions: unfolding zero ordinates removes the deterministic density and absolute height, while Hermite normal forms connect coefficient geometry to GUE-compatible roots through different derivative, shift, and degree limits. These bridges can reveal universal local interaction without certifying the real parts of zeta zeros.
historical_or_program_relation: The vertical-statistics viewpoint is refined by an explicit account of what unfolding forgets and by a coefficient-polynomial route to a compatible normal form, separating statistical universality from the pointwise RH assertion.
limits: No cited unit constructs a fixed global spectral operator or proves RH from GUE compatibility; the Hermite bridge mixes limiting parameters with different epistemic status, and local correlation laws are not a zero-line criterion.

title: Boundary averages scalarize zero information but retain a quantifier burden
claim: Averaged logarithmic boundary magnitude is a shared bridge from analytic objects to zero or value data: cyclotomic-product height is reported to probe a zeta zero-free half-plane, while Jensen's boundary average expands into Nevanlinna counting, proximity, and characteristic observables. Scalarization makes growth comparable, but the region detected depends on exact asymptotic quantifiers.
historical_or_program_relation: The cyclotomic criterion can be read as a specialized descendant of the broader boundary-mean-to-divisor program, replacing full value-distribution bookkeeping by one arithmetic family and one growth scale.
limits: The Nevanlinna unit supplies a general framework rather than the cyclotomic RH equivalence, and the cyclotomic unit explicitly lacks enough displayed quantification to justify an automatic RH specialization; no identity between their observables is claimed.

title: Logarithmic differentiation converts zero geometry into sign control
claim: Logarithmic differentiation turns multiplicative zero data into additive contributions that can be controlled by symmetry. In the Eisenstein-integral route, paired zero blocks and a height gap enforce unimodality of a scalar level-set function; in Speiser-type arguments, a nonzero sign for F′/F obstructs isolated derivative zeros on the line and supplies boundary control for matched contour counts.
historical_or_program_relation: The same analytic operation supports two historically different reformulations—line-zero theorems for shifted sums and function/derivative zero correspondences—because it exposes a one-dimensional sign interface from global products.
limits: The sign inputs are representation-specific: coarse zero-height information in the first route does not replace Gamma- or degree-dependent estimates in the second, and neither mechanism alone transfers its conclusion to arbitrary completed functions.
